data.command: Describe Turla group satellite-based covert C2

data.text:
Turla (also tracked as Uroburos, Snake, Venomous Bear, Waterbug, KRYPTON; attributed to the Russian FSB's Center 16) pioneered a command-and-control channel that runs through commercial satellite broadband downlinks instead of attacker-owned servers. Publicly documented by Symantec in September 2015 as "Satellite Turla", the channel had been in use against targets in Europe and the Middle East since roughly 2010.

The underlying trick depends on the physics of satellite internet. A consumer VSAT / gateway operator beams downstream traffic over a footprint covering thousands of square kilometres, and that stream is readable by anyone with a dish pointed at the correct transponder. Turla picked IP addresses belonging to ordinary satellite-broadband subscribers - typically customers in remote, thinly populated regions of Africa, Asia and the Middle East - and hard-coded those addresses into the victim implant as its C2 endpoints. From the victim's point of view the implant is simply exchanging traffic with another home broadband customer; nothing in the session looks like a professional C2 server.

The operators never open an inbound connection to the victim. They park a receiver inside the satellite's coverage, capture the victim's requests as those packets pass over the air, and inject the reply back into the same broadcast stream. Because the downlink is a shared broadcast, the answering packets do not have to traverse any attacker-controlled host, and the attackers' real infrastructure never appears in the victim's logs. Registration and geolocation lookups on the C2 addresses resolve to a private subscriber in a sparsely used satellite cell, which makes attribution and blocking politically awkward - the "malicious" IP belongs to an innocent third party.

Detection leans on the one unavoidable artefact: the victim must still reach out to a satellite ISP range. Useful hunts are egress to known VSAT operator netblocks from hosts that have no business talking to them, periodic beacons to residential satellite addresses that are geographically inconsistent with the host's own region, and sessions where the peer never behaves like a real server (no matching handshake from the far side, extreme and asymmetric latency, replies that appear to originate from a satellite peer). Turla has since diversified - hijacked HTTP servers and watering holes, LightNeuron's email-based C2, and the Snake implant itself, which the FBI dismantled in Operation Medusa in May 2023 - but the satellite channel remains the textbook example of evading network-based C2 detection by letting someone else's broadcast medium carry your traffic.
